questions.title: "How does Orthogonal Finetuning preserve pairwise angles between neurons during adaptation?
questions.question_body:
"I notice that Orthogonal Finetuning multiplies a frozen weight matrix \(W^0\) on the left by a learnable orthogonal matrix \(\mathbf R\). I get that a left‑multiplication by an orthonormal matrix keeps dot products unchanged (
\[ \langle \mathbf R \mathbf w_i , \mathbf R \mathbf w_j \rangle = \langle \mathbf w_i , \mathbf w_j \rangle \]), yet I’m unclear why preserving cosine similarities alone guarantees that 'semantic knowledge' learned from pre‑training stays intact.
Can someone explain mathematically what invariants are maintained during an OFT update and under what assumptions about activation functions or downstream loss functions does this help generalisation?

questions.title: "Why can't a block‑diagonal orthogonal matrix achieve classic linear transforms?
questions.question_body:
"The paper says a pure diagonal‑block form introduced in original OFT cannot approximate many useful linear transforms such as FFT or Hadamard matrices.
Since every neuron dimension belongs either entirely to one diagonal block or another, why precisely does this restriction remove expressivity?
Is it merely because cross‑block interactions are impossible, or are there deeper rank/orthogonality constraints that prevent even approximate construction of dense transforms?

questions.title: "Can someone walk through the ‘information transmission view’ used for designing sparse factorizations?
"Why ensures each butterfly component remains an exact rotation when built from 2×2 blocks?
"Exact parameter count for BOFT(m,b): comparison against OFT and LoRA
questions.question_body:
"The claim was that BOFT(m,b) trains ~\tfrac12(b-1)d m effective weights.
To solidify my understanding could you give concrete numbers?
For example take d=512 (typical transformer embedding size), b=4 and m=4—how many scalar parameters does BOFT learn?
Contrast this with original OFT (	frac12(d−1)d≈13 M forming full d-by-d rotational layer) and LoRA’s two low‐rank matrices requiring br free parameters.

questions.title: "Why standard dropout fails in BOFT while multiplicative dropout works
questions.question_body:
"LoRA commonly applies standard dropout over its low‑rank updates.
Because BOFT updates weights via successive multiplication by *orthonormal* factor layers , random dropping columns would destroy unitary properties.
Could someone step through their proposed multiplicative dropout algorithm:
– How do you choose %p₁ %p₂,
– Which butterfly blocks become identity,
– And what effect (on gradient flow / regularisation) results compared against naïve element‐wise dropping applied directly on weight matrices?

questions.title: "How does Theorem 1 establish greater expressivity for BOFT versus block‑diagonal OFT?
questions.question_body:
"The authors state ‘BOFT outperforms OFT when both use equal block size’. They claim Theorem 1 proves higher expressiveness.
Please provide intuition behind:
• Why concatenating several distinct butterfly layers introduces more degrees of freedom than one linear layer broken into static blocks;
• If possible give a tiny illustrative counterexample where a transformation realizable via high‑m Butterfly layers cannot be achieved using any single diagonal‐block rotation even when equally many trainable scalars exist.

questions.title: "Does stacking enough butterflies allow BOFT to span the full O(d)?
"Spectral properties preserved under OFT/BOFT versus LoRA – why matters?
questions.question_body:
"Paper claims multiplying left⁑ W⁰ by ⃖Rwō preserves largest singular value  largest singular norms stay fixed.
Beyond that definition,
a wide range “singular‐value spectrum” measures (e.g., spread, min/max ratio). Does OBFTOF impose further regularisation vs LoRA–and how drastic differences affect training stability / generalisation experimentally reported?

questions.title: "Can one substitute other sparse topologies instead of butterflies?
questions.question_body:
"Section 6 hints usefulness of fast network topologies beyond Cooley‑Tukey for improved factorisations.
't Is there theoretical reasoning suggesting butterflies minimize edge count among all possible directed graphs enforcing full connectivity under orthogonality constraints?
and whether other network design paradigms could yield comparable parameter gains while reducing runtime overhead?
